Since \(\vec{a}\) is directed due north and \(\vec{b}\) is directed due west, the two vectors are perpendicular to each other.
By the Pythagoras theorem,
\(|\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = \sqrt{|\vec{a}|^2+|\vec{b}|^2} = \sqrt{24^2+7^2} = \sqrt{576+49}=\sqrt{625}\)
\(\therefore |\vec{a}+\vec{b}| = 25\) units.

Let A(1, 1, 0), B(1, 0, 1), C(0, 1, 1).
\(\vec{AB} = (1-1)\hat i+(0-1)\hat j+(1-0)\hat k = -\hat j+\hat k\)
\(\vec{AC} = (0-1)\hat i+(1-1)\hat j+(1-0)\hat k = -\hat i+\hat k\)
\(\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC} = \begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\0&-1&1\\-1&0&1\end{vmatrix} = \hat i(-1-0)-\hat j(0+1)+\hat k(0-1) = -\hat i-\hat j-\hat k\)
\(|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}| = \sqrt{1+1+1}=\sqrt3\)
Area of triangle \(=\dfrac12|\vec{AB}\times\vec{AC}| = \dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\) sq units.

Let \(B \equiv (x, y, z)\). Then \(\vec{AB} = (x-1)\hat i+(y-5)\hat j+z\hat k\).
Given \(\vec{AB}=2\hat i-4\hat j+7\hat k\), comparing components:
\(x-1=2 \Rightarrow x=3\)
\(y-5=-4 \Rightarrow y=1\)
\(z=7\)
\(\therefore\) the terminal point is \(B \equiv (3, 1, 7)\).

A(3, 2, -4), B(9, 8, -10), C(-2, -3, 1)
\(\vec{AB} = (9-3)\hat i+(8-2)\hat j+(-10+4)\hat k = 6\hat i+6\hat j-6\hat k\)
\(\vec{AC} = (-2-3)\hat i+(-3-2)\hat j+(1+4)\hat k = -5\hat i-5\hat j+5\hat k\)
Here \(\vec{AC} = -\dfrac{5}{6}\vec{AB}\), so \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{AC}\) are parallel vectors having the point A in common.
\(\therefore\) A, B, C are collinear.

P(4, 5, 2), Q(3, 2, 4), R(5, 8, 0)
\(\vec{PQ} = (3-4)\hat i+(2-5)\hat j+(4-2)\hat k = -\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k\)
\(\vec{PR} = (5-4)\hat i+(8-5)\hat j+(0-2)\hat k = \hat i+3\hat j-2\hat k\)
Here \(\vec{PR} = -\vec{PQ}\), so \(\vec{PQ}\) and \(\vec{PR}\) are parallel vectors having the point P in common.
\(\therefore\) P, Q, R are collinear.

The vectors \(2\hat i-q\hat j+3\hat k\) and \(4\hat i-5\hat j+6\hat k\) are collinear, so their corresponding components are proportional:
\(\dfrac{2}{4}=\dfrac{-q}{-5}=\dfrac{3}{6}\)
From the first and third ratios, \(\dfrac24=\dfrac12\), so
\(\dfrac{-q}{-5}=\dfrac12 \Rightarrow \dfrac{q}{5}=\dfrac12 \Rightarrow q=\dfrac52\).

A(1, -1, 1), B(-1, 1, 1), C(1, 1, 1), D(2, -3, 4)
\(\vec{AB} = -2\hat i+2\hat j\), \(\vec{AC} = 2\hat j\), \(\vec{AD} = \hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k\)
Four points are coplanar iff the scalar triple product \([\vec{AB}\ \vec{AC}\ \vec{AD}]=0\).
\(\vec{AC}\times\vec{AD}=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\0&2&0\\1&-2&3\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(6-0)-\hat j(0-0)+\hat k(0-2)=6\hat i-2\hat k\)
\(\vec{AB}\cdot(\vec{AC}\times\vec{AD}) = (-2)(6)+(2)(0)+(0)(-2) = -12 \neq 0\)
Since the scalar triple product is not zero, the four points A, B, C, D are **not coplanar**.

Let \(-\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k = x(2\hat i+\hat j-4\hat k)+y(2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k)+z(3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k)\).
Comparing coefficients of \(\hat i, \hat j, \hat k\):
\(2x+2y+3z=-1\) ... (i)
\(x-y+z=-3\) ... (ii)
\(-4x+3y-2z=4\) ... (iii)
Solving (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously gives \(x=2,\ y=2,\ z=-3\)
(Check: \(2(2)+2(2)+3(-3)=-1\); \(2-2+(-3)=-3\); \(-4(2)+3(2)-2(-3)=4\) -- all satisfied.)
\(\therefore -\hat i-3\hat j+4\hat k = 2(2\hat i+\hat j-4\hat k)+2(2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k)-3(3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k)\).

By the triangle (chain) law,
\(\vec{PR} = \vec{PQ}+\vec{QR} = 2\vec a+2\vec b\).

M is the midpoint of PR, so
\(\vec{PM} = \dfrac12\vec{PR} = \dfrac12(2\vec a+2\vec b) = \vec a+\vec b\).
\(\vec{QM} = \vec{QP}+\vec{PM} = -2\vec a+(\vec a+\vec b) = \vec b-\vec a\).

Take O as the origin, so the position vectors of A and B are \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\).
A regular hexagon OABCDE is centrally symmetric about its centre, so opposite sides are equal in length, parallel, and oppositely directed:
\(\vec{CD}=-\vec{OA}, \quad \vec{DE}=-\vec{AB}, \quad \vec{EO}=-\vec{BC}\)
Using this property together with \(\vec{AB}=\vec b-\vec a\), the position vectors of the remaining vertices (relative to O) work out to:
\(\vec{OC} = 2\vec b-2\vec a\)
\(\vec{OD} = 2\vec b-3\vec a\)
\(\vec{OE} = \vec b-2\vec a\)
(Check: \(\vec{CD}=\vec{OD}-\vec{OC}=-\vec a=-\vec{OA}\), confirming the opposite-side property.)

Take O (the centre of the hexagon) as the origin. In a regular hexagon ABCDEF, D is diametrically opposite A through the centre O, so O is the midpoint of AD; similarly O is the midpoint of BE and of CF.
Hence, with position vectors taken relative to O: \(\vec D=-\vec A,\ \vec E=-\vec B,\ \vec F=-\vec C\).
Now,
\(\vec{AB}+\vec{AC}+\vec{AD}+\vec{AE}+\vec{AF}\)
\(=(\vec B-\vec A)+(\vec C-\vec A)+(\vec D-\vec A)+(\vec E-\vec A)+(\vec F-\vec A)\)
\(=(\vec B-\vec A)+(\vec C-\vec A)+(-\vec A-\vec A)+(-\vec B-\vec A)+(-\vec C-\vec A)\)
\(=-6\vec A\)
Also \(\vec{AO}=\vec O-\vec A=-\vec A\) (O is the origin), so \(-6\vec A = 6\vec{AO}\).
\(\therefore \vec{AB}+\vec{AC}+\vec{AD}+\vec{AE}+\vec{AF}=6\vec{AO}\), as required.

Let \(\vec p=2\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k,\ \vec q=-3\hat i+3\hat j+2\hat k,\ \vec r=3\hat i+4\hat k\).
Three vectors, taken in order and placed head to tail, form a triangle if and only if their sum is the zero vector.
\(\vec p+\vec q+\vec r = (2-3+3)\hat i+(2+3+0)\hat j+(3+2+4)\hat k = 2\hat i+5\hat j+9\hat k \neq \vec 0\)
Since the sum is not the zero vector, the given vectors **do not form a triangle**.

Since S is the midpoint of QR, by the triangle law of addition
\(\vec{QR}=\vec{QP}+\vec{PR}=\vec a+\vec b\)
As S is the midpoint of QR,
\(\vec{QS}=\vec{SR}=\dfrac12\vec{QR}=\dfrac12(\vec a+\vec b)\)
\(\therefore \vec d = \vec{SR} = \dfrac12(\vec a+\vec b)\)
Also, using the triangle law in \(\Delta PQS\),
\(\vec{PS}=\vec{PQ}+\vec{QS}=-\vec a+\dfrac12(\vec a+\vec b)=\dfrac12(\vec b-\vec a)\)
\(\therefore \vec c = \dfrac12(\vec b-\vec a)\).

\(|\vec a| = \sqrt{1^2+(-2)^2}=\sqrt5\)
Unit vector along \(\vec a\): \(\hat a=\dfrac{\hat i-2\hat j}{\sqrt5}\)
Required vector \(=7\hat a = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt5}(\hat i-2\hat j) = \dfrac{7\sqrt5}{5}\hat i-\dfrac{14\sqrt5}{5}\hat j\).
Distance of the point (4, -2, 6) from the XY-plane \(=|z|=6\) units.
Distance of the point (4, -2, 6) from the YZ-plane \(=|x|=4\) units.
Distance of the point (4, -2, 6) from the XZ-plane \(=|y|=2\) units.
Distance of the point (4, -2, 6) from the X-axis \(=\sqrt{y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{(-2)^2+6^2}=\sqrt{4+36}=\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}\) units.
Distance of the point (4, -2, 6) from the Y-axis \(=\sqrt{x^2+z^2}=\sqrt{16+36}=\sqrt{52}=2\sqrt{13}\) units.
Distance of the point (4, -2, 6) from the Z-axis \(=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5\) units.

Three units behind the YZ-plane \(\Rightarrow x=-3\)
Four units to the right of the XZ-plane \(\Rightarrow y=4\)
Five units above the XY-plane \(\Rightarrow z=5\)
\(\therefore\) the point is \((-3, 4, 5)\).

In the YZ-plane \(\Rightarrow x=0\)
One unit to the right of the XZ-plane \(\Rightarrow y=1\)
Six units above the XY-plane \(\Rightarrow z=6\)
\(\therefore\) the point is \((0, 1, 6)\).

Take A as the origin, so \(\vec{AB}=\vec p\).
Since \(\vec{BC}=\vec q\), \(\vec{AC}=\vec{AB}+\vec{BC}=\vec p+\vec q\).
Since DC is parallel to AB in the same sense, with \(DC=3AB\), \(\vec{DC}=3\vec p\), so \(\vec{CD}=-3\vec p\).
\(\vec{AD}=\vec{AC}+\vec{CD}=(\vec p+\vec q)-3\vec p=\vec q-2\vec p\)
M is the midpoint of DC, so
\(\vec{AM}=\dfrac{\vec{AD}+\vec{AC}}{2}=\dfrac{(\vec q-2\vec p)+(\vec p+\vec q)}{2}=\dfrac{2\vec q-\vec p}{2}=\vec q-\dfrac12\vec p\).

From part (i), \(\vec{AD}=\vec q-2\vec p\) and \(\vec{AB}=\vec p\).
\(\vec{BD}=\vec{AD}-\vec{AB}=(\vec q-2\vec p)-\vec p=\vec q-3\vec p\).

From part (i), \(\vec{AM}=\vec q-\dfrac12\vec p\) and \(\vec{AB}=\vec p\).
\(\vec{MB}=\vec{AB}-\vec{AM}=\vec p-\left(\vec q-\dfrac12\vec p\right)=\dfrac32\vec p-\vec q\).

From part (i), \(\vec{AD}=\vec q-2\vec p\).
\(\vec{DA}=-\vec{AD}=-(\vec q-2\vec p)=2\vec p-\vec q\).

For \(y=x^2\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x\). At the point (2, 4), the slope of the tangent \(=2(2)=4\).
A direction vector along the tangent (run 1, rise 4) is \(\hat i+4\hat j\).
\(|\hat i+4\hat j|=\sqrt{1+16}=\sqrt{17}\)
\(\therefore\) the required unit vectors are \(\pm\dfrac{\hat i+4\hat j}{\sqrt{17}}\).

Let \(\hat i+4\hat j-4\hat k=x(2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k)+y(\hat i-2\hat j+4\hat k)+z(-\hat i+3\hat j-5\hat k)\).
Comparing coefficients:
\(2x+y-z=1\) ... (i)
\(-x-2y+3z=4\) ... (ii)
\(3x+4y-5z=-4\) ... (iii)
Solving (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously gives \(x=1,\ y=2,\ z=3\)
(Check: \(2(1)+2-3=1\); \(-1-2(2)+3(3)=4\); \(3(1)+4(2)-5(3)=-4\) -- all satisfied.)
\(\therefore \hat i+4\hat j-4\hat k=(2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k)+2(\hat i-2\hat j+4\hat k)+3(-\hat i+3\hat j-5\hat k)\).

Let \(\hat a=\dfrac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}\) and \(\hat b=\dfrac{\vec b}{|\vec b|}\) be the unit vectors along \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) respectively.
Consider the parallelogram formed by \(\hat a\) and \(\hat b\) as adjacent sides. Since \(|\hat a|=|\hat b|=1\), this parallelogram is a rhombus.
The diagonal of a rhombus bisects the angle between its sides, so the vector \(\hat a+\hat b\) lies along the bisector of \(\angle AOB\).
Any vector along this bisector direction is a scalar multiple of \(\hat a+\hat b\):
\(\vec d=\lambda(\hat a+\hat b)=\lambda\left(\dfrac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}+\dfrac{\vec b}{|\vec b|}\right)\), where \(\lambda \in \mathbb R\), as required.

Let A, B, C be three consecutive vertices of parallelogram ABCD with position vectors \(\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k\), \(\vec b=\hat i+3\hat j+5\hat k\), \(\vec c=7\hat i+9\hat j+11\hat k\); let D have position vector \(\vec d\).
In a parallelogram, the diagonals bisect each other, so the midpoint of AC equals the midpoint of BD:
\(\dfrac{\vec a+\vec c}{2}=\dfrac{\vec b+\vec d}{2}\)
\(\Rightarrow \vec d=\vec a+\vec c-\vec b=(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)+(7\hat i+9\hat j+11\hat k)-(\hat i+3\hat j+5\hat k)\)
\(=7\hat i+7\hat j+7\hat k\)
\(\therefore\) the position vector of the fourth vertex D is \(7\hat i+7\hat j+7\hat k\).

Take A as the origin; let B, C, D, E have position vectors \(\vec b,\vec c,\vec d,\vec e\).
\(\vec{AB}=\vec b,\ \vec{AE}=\vec e,\ \vec{BC}=\vec c-\vec b,\ \vec{DC}=\vec c-\vec d,\ \vec{ED}=\vec d-\vec e\)
Adding all five vectors:
\(\vec{AB}+\vec{AE}+\vec{BC}+\vec{DC}+\vec{ED}\)
\(=\vec b+\vec e+(\vec c-\vec b)+(\vec c-\vec d)+(\vec d-\vec e)\)
\(=2\vec c\)
Since \(\vec{AC}=\vec c\) (A is the origin), \(2\vec c=2\vec{AC}\).
\(\therefore \vec{AB}+\vec{AE}+\vec{BC}+\vec{DC}+\vec{ED}=2\vec{AC}\), as required.

Take A as the origin, so the position vectors of B, C, D are \(\vec{AB}\), \(\vec{AC}=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k\), \(\vec{AD}\).
Since ABCD is a parallelogram, \(\vec{AB}=\vec{DC}=\vec{AC}-\vec{AD}\), so \(\vec{AD}=\vec{AC}-\vec{AB}\).
Also \(\vec{BD}=\vec{AD}-\vec{AB}=(\vec{AC}-\vec{AB})-\vec{AB}=\vec{AC}-2\vec{AB}\)
\(\Rightarrow 2\vec{AB}=\vec{AC}-\vec{BD}=(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)-(-6\hat i+7\hat j-2\hat k)=8\hat i-4\hat j+6\hat k\)
\(\Rightarrow \vec{AB}=4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k\)
Then \(\vec{AD}=\vec{AC}-\vec{AB}=(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)-(4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k)=-2\hat i+5\hat j+\hat k\)
\(\therefore \vec{AB}=4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k,\quad \vec{AD}=-2\hat i+5\hat j+\hat k\).

Let the two sides, taken in the same order, be \(\vec{AB}=\hat i+2\hat j\) and \(\vec{BC}=\hat i+\hat k\).
Since the three sides of a triangle taken in order sum to the zero vector, \(\vec{AB}+\vec{BC}+\vec{CA}=\vec 0\).
\(\vec{CA}=-(\vec{AB}+\vec{BC})=-\big[(\hat i+2\hat j)+(\hat i+\hat k)\big]=-(2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k)\)
\(|\vec{CA}|=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-2)^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{4+4+1}=\sqrt9=3\)
\(\therefore\) the length of the third side is 3 units.

Let the adjacent sides of the parallelogram be \(\vec p=3\hat i+4\hat j-5\hat k\) and \(\vec q=-2\hat j+7\hat k\).
The diagonals of the parallelogram are \(\vec p+\vec q\) and \(\vec p-\vec q\):
\(\vec p+\vec q=3\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k, \quad |\vec p+\vec q|=\sqrt{9+4+4}=\sqrt{17}\)
\(\vec p-\vec q=3\hat i+6\hat j-12\hat k, \quad |\vec p-\vec q|=\sqrt{9+36+144}=\sqrt{189}=3\sqrt{21}\)
Unit vectors along the diagonals:
\(\dfrac{3\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k}{\sqrt{17}}\) and \(\dfrac{3\hat i+6\hat j-12\hat k}{3\sqrt{21}}=\dfrac{\hat i+2\hat j-4\hat k}{\sqrt{21}}\).
